# 1. Load packages and NHANES datasets

This analysis uses NHANES 2017–2018 data to examine the association between urinary 3-PBA and serum AMH concentrations among women aged 20-44 years.

```{r setup, message=FALSE}
library(haven)
library(survey)
```

## Download NHANES datasets
```{r analysis-1}
# NHANES 2017-2018 data location
base <- "https://wwwn.cdc.gov/Nchs/Data/Nhanes/Public/2017/DataFiles/"

# Download and organize the seven datasets
nhanes <- list(
  pba = read_xpt(paste0(base, "UPHOPM_J.xpt")),
  amh = read_xpt(paste0(base, "SSTST_J.xpt")),
  demo = read_xpt(paste0(base, "DEMO_J.xpt")),
  bmi = read_xpt(paste0(base, "BMX_J.xpt")),
  creatinine = read_xpt(paste0(base, "ALB_CR_J.xpt")),
  smoking = read_xpt(paste0(base, "SMQ_J.xpt")),
  hormones = read_xpt(paste0(base, "RHQ_J.xpt"))
)

# Confirm which datasets loaded
names(nhanes)
```

# 2. Merge datasets and select variables

The NHANES datasets will be merged using SEQN, the unique participant identifier. Only variables needed for the study will be retained.

```{r analysis-2}
# Select demographic variables
data <- nhanes$demo[, c(
  "SEQN", "RIAGENDR", "RIDAGEYR", "RIDEXPRG",
  "RIDRETH3", "DMDEDUC2", "INDFMPIR",
  "SDMVSTRA", "SDMVPSU"
)]

# Merge exposure and outcome
data <- merge(data, nhanes$pba[, c("SEQN", "URXOPM", "WTSB2YR")],
              by = "SEQN", all.x = TRUE)


data <- merge(data, nhanes$amh[, c("SEQN", "SSTAMH")],
              by = "SEQN", all.x = TRUE)

# Merge potential confounders
data <- merge(data, nhanes$bmi[, c("SEQN", "BMXBMI")],
              by = "SEQN", all.x = TRUE)

data <- merge(data, nhanes$creatinine[, c("SEQN", "URXUCR")],
              by = "SEQN", all.x = TRUE)

data <- merge(data, nhanes$smoking[, c("SEQN", "SMQ020")],
              by = "SEQN", all.x = TRUE)

data <- merge(data, nhanes$hormones[, c("SEQN", "RHQ420")],
              by = "SEQN", all.x = TRUE)

# Check the dimensions of the combined dataset
dim(data)
```

# 3. Apply eligibility criteria and document exclusions

The study population consists of nonpregnant women aged 20-44 years with available urinary 3-PBA and serum AMH measurements. Participant counts are recorded at each stage of selection. 

Women whose pregnancy status could not be ascertained are excluded along with those confirmed pregnant.

```{r pregnancy-status}
# Check pregnancy status among women aged 20–44
table(
  data$RIDEXPRG[data$RIAGENDR == 2 &
                  data$RIDAGEYR >= 20 &
                  data$RIDAGEYR <= 44],
  useNA = "always")
```
```{r analysis-3}
# Count participants remaining after each criterion
flow <- data.frame(
  Stage = c(
    "All NHANES participants",
    "Female participants",
    "Women aged 20-44",
    "Confirmed nonpregnant",
    "Available 3-PBA and AMH"
  ),
  N = c(
    nrow(data),
    sum(data$RIAGENDR == 2, na.rm = TRUE),
    sum(data$RIAGENDR == 2 &
        data$RIDAGEYR >= 20 &
        data$RIDAGEYR <= 44, na.rm = TRUE),
    sum(data$RIAGENDR == 2 &
        data$RIDAGEYR >= 20 &
        data$RIDAGEYR <= 44 &
        data$RIDEXPRG == 2, na.rm = TRUE),
    sum(data$RIAGENDR == 2 &
        data$RIDAGEYR >= 20 &
        data$RIDAGEYR <= 44 &
        data$RIDEXPRG == 2 &
        !is.na(data$URXOPM) &
        !is.na(data$SSTAMH), na.rm = TRUE)))

# Create the eligible study sample
sample <- subset(
  data,
  RIAGENDR == 2 &
    RIDAGEYR >= 20 &
    RIDAGEYR <= 44 &
    RIDEXPRG == 2 &
    !is.na(URXOPM) &
    !is.na(SSTAMH))

# Display participant counts
flow
```

# 4. Assess missing data and variable coding

Missing values are assessed among eligible participants before selecting covariates for regression models.
```{r analysis-4}
# Count missing values for each variable in the eligible sample
colSums(is.na(sample))
```
## Check variable coding and biomarker distributions

```{r analysis-5}
# Examine response codes before recoding variables
table(sample$SMQ020, useNA = "always")
table(sample$RHQ420, useNA = "always")
table(sample$DMDEDUC2, useNA = "always")


# Summarize the exposure and outcome distributions
summary(sample$URXOPM)
summary(sample$SSTAMH)

# Check whether either variable contains zero or negative values
sum(sample$URXOPM <= 0, na.rm = TRUE)
sum(sample$SSTAMH <= 0, na.rm = TRUE)

```
Among 253 women, urinary 3-PBA (µg/L) had an unweighted median of 0.75 (IQR 0.35–1.60), mean of 2.55, and maximum of 110. Serum AMH (ng/mL) had an unweighted median of 2.39 (IQR 1.07–4.07), mean of 2.89, and maximum of 22.29. Both distributions were right-skewed, and neither contained nonpositive values.

Histograms were used to examine the distributions of urinary 3-PBA and serum AMH before selecting transformations for regression analysis.

```{r analysis-6}
# Urinary 3-PBA distribution
hist(sample$URXOPM,
     breaks = 25,
     col = "#4C78A8",
     border = "white",
     main = "Distribution of Urinary 3-PBA",
     xlab = "Urinary 3-PBA (µg/L)")

# Serum AMH distribution
hist(sample$SSTAMH,

```

# 5. Specify NHANES survey design

NHANES uses a complex, multistage sampling design. The analysis will account for environmental subsample weights, sampling strata, and primary sampling units (PSU).
```{r analysis-7}

# Check the laboratory subsample weights
summary(sample$WTSB2YR)

# Count missing weights
sum(is.na(sample$WTSB2YR))

# Count zero or negative weights
sum(sample$WTSB2YR <= 0, na.rm = TRUE)
```
```{r analysis-8}
# Define the design among participants with valid lab weights
design <- svydesign(
  ids = ~SDMVPSU,
  strata = ~SDMVSTRA,
  weights = ~WTSB2YR,
  nest = TRUE,
  data = subset(data, !is.na(WTSB2YR) & WTSB2YR > 0))

# Restrict to our eligible study population
design <- subset(
  design,
  RIAGENDR == 2 &
    RIDAGEYR >= 20 &
    RIDAGEYR <= 44 &
    RIDEXPRG == 2 &
    !is.na(URXOPM) &
    !is.na(SSTAMH))

# Verify the eligible sample size
nrow(design$variables)
```

# 6. Generate Table 1 and descriptive statistics
Table 1 describes the 253 eligible women with urinary 3-PBA
and serum AMH measurements. Continuous characteristics are
summarized using survey-weighted means or medians, and
categorical characteristics using unweighted counts and
survey-weighted percentages. Smoking and birth control pill
history are descriptive variables, not regression covariates.

```{r}
# Format survey-weighted means and standard errors
mean_se <- function(variable) {
  x <- svymean(as.formula(paste0("~", variable)),
               design, na.rm = TRUE)
  sprintf("%.2f (%.2f)", coef(x)[1], SE(x)[1])
}

# Format survey-weighted median and interquartile range
median_iqr <- function(variable) {
  x <- svyquantile(
    as.formula(paste0("~", variable)),
    design,
    quantiles = c(0.25, 0.50, 0.75),
    na.rm = TRUE,
    ci = FALSE
  )
  q <- as.numeric(coef(x))
  sprintf("%.2f (%.2f–%.2f)", q[2], q[1], q[3])
}

# Format unweighted count and survey-weighted percentage
category_result <- function(variable, code) {
  n <- sum(sample[[variable]] == code, na.rm = TRUE)
  weighted <- svytable(
    as.formula(paste0("~", variable)), design
  )
  pct <- 100 * as.numeric(weighted[as.character(code)]) /
    sum(weighted)
  sprintf("%d (%.1f%%)", n, pct)
}

# Race/ethnicity categories in NHANES
race_codes <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7)
race_labels <- c(
  "  Mexican American",
  "  Other Hispanic",
  "  Non-Hispanic White",
  "  Non-Hispanic Black",
  "  Non-Hispanic Asian",
  "  Other / Multiracial"
)

# Education categories in NHANES
education_codes <- 1:5
education_labels <- c(
  "  Less than 9th grade",
  "  9th–11th grade",
  "  High school graduate / GED",
  "  Some college / Associate degree",
  "  College graduate or above"
)

# Assemble Table 1
table1 <- data.frame(
  Characteristic = c(
    "Age (years), mean (SE)",
    "BMI (kg/m²), mean (SE)",
    "Urinary 3-PBA (µg/L), median (Q1–Q3)",
    "Serum AMH (ng/mL), median (Q1–Q3)",
    "Urinary creatinine (mg/dL), median (Q1–Q3)",
    "Income-to-poverty ratio, mean (SE)",
    "Race/ethnicity, n (weighted %)",
    race_labels,
    "Education, n (weighted %)",
    education_labels,
    "Ever smoked ≥100 cigarettes, Yes, n (weighted %)",
    "Ever used birth control pills, Yes, n (weighted %)"
  ),
  Result = c(
    mean_se("RIDAGEYR"),
    mean_se("BMXBMI"),
    median_iqr("URXOPM"),
    median_iqr("SSTAMH"),
    median_iqr("URXUCR"),
    mean_se("INDFMPIR"),
    "",
    sapply(race_codes, function(x)
      category_result("RIDRETH3", x)),
    "",
    sapply(education_codes, function(x)
      category_result("DMDEDUC2", x)),
    category_result("SMQ020", 1),
    category_result("RHQ420", 1)
  )
)

knitr::kable(
  table1,
  col.names = c("Characteristic", "Eligible sample (N = 253)"),
  caption = "Table 1. Characteristics of eligible women, NHANES 2017–2018"
)
```

## 7. Visualize the exposure–outcome relationship

An unweighted scatterplot was used to examine the relationship between urinary 3-PBA and serum AMH among the 253 eligible participants. Because urinary 3-PBA was right-skewed, it was natural-log transformed to improve visualization and match the exposure transformation used in the regression models. Serum AMH was retained on its original scale (ng/mL) for interpretation.

```{r scatterplot-log-pba}
# Log-transformed 3-PBA versus original-scale AMH
plot(
  log(sample$URXOPM), sample$SSTAMH,
  pch = 16,
  col = adjustcolor("#4C78A8", alpha.f = 0.5),
  xlab = "Natural log of urinary 3-PBA (µg/L)",
  ylab = "Serum AMH (ng/mL)",
  main = "Log urinary 3-PBA and serum AMH"
)
```

The scatterplot shows substantial variability in serum AMH across log-transformed urinary 3-PBA concentrations, without a clear visual linear relationship. Several observations have relatively high AMH concentrations, which will be considered during regression diagnostics.

## 8. Urine-dilution-adjusted and multivariable regression models

I fitted survey-weighted linear regression models to evaluate the association between urinary 3-PBA and serum AMH. Urinary 3-PBA was natural-log-transformed because of its right-skewed distribution.

The first model included urinary 3-PBA and urinary creatinine (urine-dilution-adjusted model). The primary multivariable model additionally adjusted for age and family income-to-poverty ratio (PIR), based on the literature-informed DAG. Both models use the same complete-case sample.

Both models used the NHANES environmental subsample weights, strata, and primary sampling units.

```{r regression-models}
# Create log-transformed urinary 3-PBA within the survey design
design <- update(design, log_pba = log(URXOPM))

# Restrict both models to participants with complete covariate data
design_models <- subset(
  design,
  !is.na(INDFMPIR) & !is.na(URXUCR) & !is.na(RIDAGEYR))

# Model 1: Exposure association, adjusted for urine dilution
model_unadjusted <- svyglm(
  SSTAMH ~ log_pba + URXUCR,
  design = design_models)

# Model 2: Additionally adjusted for DAG-selected confounders
model_adjusted <- svyglm(
  SSTAMH ~ log_pba + URXUCR + RIDAGEYR + INDFMPIR,
  design = design_models)

# Display regression results
summary(model_unadjusted)
summary(model_adjusted)
confint(model_adjusted)["log_pba", ]

# Check the sample size used in both models
nrow(design_models$variables)
```
## 9. Effect modification by age

I examined whether age modified the association between urinary 3-PBA and serum AMH by including an interaction term between log-transformed 3-PBA and age in the survey-weighted adjusted model.

```{r age-interaction}
# Center age at 30 years for easier interpretation
design_models <- update(
  design_models,
  age_centered = RIDAGEYR - 30)

# Fit the adjusted model with an age-by-3-PBA interaction
model_interaction <- svyglm(
  SSTAMH ~ log_pba * age_centered + URXUCR + INDFMPIR,
  design = design_models)

# Display the results
summary(model_interaction)


confint(model_interaction)["log_pba:age_centered", ]
```

The following figure shows model-predicted AMH at ages 20, 30, and 40, holding urinary creatinine and PIR at their sample medians. The plotted exposure range is 0.1–10 µg/L for readability; these are model predictions, not age-group averages.

```{r age-interaction-figure}
# Create a grid of exposure values and selected ages
prediction_data <- expand.grid(
  URXOPM = exp(seq(log(0.1), log(10), length.out = 100)),
  RIDAGEYR = c(20, 30, 40))

# Match the predictors used in the interaction model
prediction_data$log_pba <- log(prediction_data$URXOPM)
prediction_data$age_centered <- prediction_data$RIDAGEYR - 30

# Hold other covariates constant at their sample medians
prediction_data$URXUCR <- median(design_models$variables$URXUCR)
prediction_data$INDFMPIR <- median(design_models$variables$INDFMPIR)

# Calculate predicted AMH from the fitted interaction model
prediction_data$predicted_amh <- predict(
  model_interaction,
  newdata = prediction_data,
  type = "response")

# Plot age-specific predicted relationships
par(mar = c(5, 5, 4, 9), xpd = TRUE)
plot(
  NA,
  xlim = range(prediction_data$URXOPM),
  ylim = range(prediction_data$predicted_amh),
  log = "x",
  xlab = "Urinary 3-PBA (µg/L, log scale)",
  ylab = "Predicted serum AMH (ng/mL)",
  main = "Predicted 3-PBA–AMH association by age")

age_colors <- c("#4C78A8", "#F58518", "#54A24B")

for (i in seq_along(c(20, 30, 40))) {
  age <- c(20, 30, 40)[i]
  d <- subset(prediction_data, RIDAGEYR == age)

  lines(
    d$URXOPM,
    d$predicted_amh,
    col = age_colors[i],
    lwd = 2)}

legend(
  "topright",
  inset = c(-0.28, 0),
  legend = c("Age 20", "Age 30", "Age 40"),
  col = age_colors,
  lwd = 2,
  bty = "n")

# Restore default plotting settings
par(mar = c(5, 4, 4, 2) + 0.1, xpd = FALSE)
```
## 10. Regression diagnostics
### 10.1 Residuals versus fitted values
```{r residuals-fitted}
# Extract fitted values and residuals from the adjusted model
plot(
  fitted(model_adjusted),
  residuals(model_adjusted),
  pch = 16,
  col = adjustcolor("#4C78A8", alpha.f = 0.5),
  xlab = "Fitted serum AMH (ng/mL)",
  ylab = "Residuals (ng/mL)",
  main = "Residuals versus fitted values"
)

# Reference line for zero residual
abline(h = 0, col = "#E45756", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
```

### 10.2 Normal Q–Q plot

```{r residuals-qq}
qqnorm(
  residuals(model_adjusted),
  pch = 16,
  col = adjustcolor("#4C78A8", alpha.f = 0.5),
  main = "Normal Q-Q plot of adjusted model residuals"
)

qqline(
  residuals(model_adjusted),
  col = "#E45756",
  lwd = 2
)
```

The original-scale model showed a pronounced upper residual tail and evidence of nonconstant residual spread. These findings are documented as limitations; the primary outcome remains AMH in ng/mL for direct interpretation.

### 10.3 Residuals versus continuous predictors

```{r residuals-predictors}
# Check residual patterns against continuous predictors
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

plot(
  design_models$variables$log_pba,
  residuals(model_adjusted),
  pch = 16,
  col = adjustcolor("#4C78A8", alpha.f = 0.5),
  xlab = "Log urinary 3-PBA",
  ylab = "Residuals (ng/mL)",
  main = "Residuals vs. log 3-PBA"
)
abline(h = 0, col = "#E45756", lty = 2)

plot(
  design_models$variables$RIDAGEYR,
  residuals(model_adjusted),
  pch = 16,
  col = adjustcolor("#4C78A8", alpha.f = 0.5),
  xlab = "Age (years)",
  ylab = "Residuals (ng/mL)",
  main = "Residuals vs. age"
)
abline(h = 0, col = "#E45756", lty = 2)

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

### 10.4 Approximate influence screening

Cook’s distance and DFBETAs are calculated from an auxiliary sampling-weighted linear model with the same formula. These are screening diagnostics, not fully survey-design-based influence measures. Screening thresholds are not deletion rules.

```{r cooks-distance}
# Auxiliary model for approximate influence screening
diagnostic_model <- lm(
  SSTAMH ~ log_pba + URXUCR + RIDAGEYR + INDFMPIR,
  data = design_models$variables,
  weights = WTSB2YR
)

# Calculate Cook's distance
cooks <- cooks.distance(diagnostic_model)

plot(
  cooks,
  type = "h",
  col = "#4C78A8",
  lwd = 2,
  xlab = "Observation index",
  ylab = "Cook's distance",
  main = "Cook's distance: influence screening"
)

abline(
  h = 4 / length(cooks),
  col = "#E45756",
  lty = 2,
  lwd = 2
)


# Display the 10 largest Cook's distances
head(sort(cooks, decreasing = TRUE), 10)

# Count observations above the screening threshold
sum(cooks > 4 / length(cooks))
```
```{r pba-dfbetas}
# DFBETAs for the urinary 3-PBA coefficient
pba_dfbetas <- dfbetas(diagnostic_model)[, "log_pba"]

# Display the 10 largest absolute values
head(sort(abs(pba_dfbetas), decreasing = TRUE), 10)

# Conventional screening threshold
2 / sqrt(length(pba_dfbetas))
```
```{r influential-observations}
# Identify observations exceeding the DFBETA threshold
influential <- which(abs(pba_dfbetas) > 2 / sqrt(length(pba_dfbetas)))

# Display their exposure, outcome, and relevant covariates
design_models$variables[influential,
  c("SEQN", "URXOPM", "SSTAMH", "RIDAGEYR", "URXUCR", "INDFMPIR", "WTSB2YR")
]
```

### 10.5 Exploratory influence sensitivity check

The primary analysis retains all eligible observations. The following exploratory comparison assesses how the exposure coefficient changes when the eight observations flagged by the auxiliary DFBETA screen are temporarily excluded.

```{r influence-sensitivity}
# Compare the primary exposure coefficient with a sensitivity estimate
# excluding the eight observations flagged by DFBETAs

coef(model_adjusted)["log_pba"]

coef(
  svyglm(
    SSTAMH ~ log_pba + URXUCR + RIDAGEYR + INDFMPIR,
    design = subset(
      design_models,
      !(SEQN %in% design_models$variables$SEQN[influential])
    )
  )
)["log_pba"]

confint(
  svyglm(
    SSTAMH ~ log_pba + URXUCR + RIDAGEYR + INDFMPIR,
    design = subset(
      design_models,
      !(SEQN %in% design_models$variables$SEQN[influential])
    )
  )
)["log_pba", ]
```


The primary adjusted exposure coefficient was −0.0463 (223 participants); the exploratory exclusion estimate was −0.0971 (215 participants). The magnitude changed, but both estimates were negative. The screening method and sensitivity comparison do not establish that the excluded observations were erroneous.

## 11. Sensitivity analysis: Race/ethnicity adjustment

We conducted a sensitivity analysis additionally adjusting for
race/ethnicity to assess whether the estimated association between
urinary 3-PBA and serum AMH was sensitive to this adjustment.
Race/ethnicity was treated as a categorical variable.

```{r}
# Fit sensitivity model with race/ethnicity adjustment
model_ethnicity <- svyglm(
  SSTAMH ~ log_pba + URXUCR + RIDAGEYR + INDFMPIR +
    factor(RIDRETH3),
  design = design_models
)

# Compare exposure coefficients and confidence intervals
coef(model_adjusted)["log_pba"]
confint(model_adjusted)["log_pba", ]

coef(model_ethnicity)["log_pba"]
confint(model_ethnicity)["log_pba", ]
```
